claims.text: High-strain deformation can produce an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous near-surface layer in CoCrFeMnNi-type high-entropy alloys.
Local chemical-order variations promote formation of the near-surface layer.
The ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous layer acts as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Formation of this layer is the primary mechanism governing enhanced hardness and strength in dynamically amorphizing HEAs.
Single-phase, coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi is a suitable initially soft baseline material.
The baseline material has minimal preexisting amorphous regions.
Ultra-high-vacuum testing mitigates oxidation and mixed metal-oxide-film formation.
Under high localized strain, the alloy undergoes a dynamic crystalline-to-amorphous transformation.
Dynamic amorphization occurs preferentially in regions of high grain-boundary energy.
Local chemical ordering or short-range-order fluctuations create high-energy barriers to dislocation propagation.
The resulting ultrafine or amorphous layer produces inverse Hall–Petch-related, grain-size-dependent shear-strength behavior.
The treated specimens will have approximately 20–30% greater nanoindentation hardness than the baseline.
The treated specimens will have greater yield strength than the coarse-grained baseline.
Microscopy of treated specimens will reveal a newly formed ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous near-surface layer.
CrMnFeCoNi strength can arise from a synergy of multiple dislocation and deformation mechanisms.
claims.field: relevance of cited evidence to mechanism

claims.text: The proposed mechanism should dominate only for chemistries, strain rates, and environments that favor dynamic amorphization and should be less applicable when oxidation or other mechanisms dominate.
